title: No pianos or recordings; Mello's own band after World War I
summary: Mello explains why they played without pianos or records, then describes his own post-WWI band with Joe Castro and a lucrative out-of-town job, and Leonce's last years.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Did they have many piano players in those days? They had a few.

They never had too many of them, though. They had a few of them. But we didn't need no piano. Jacqueline never thought that we could, none did I. I didn't think. In the first place, where we played, we played mostly in the open. And when we played in a place in the hall, so they had pianos. But they were so low that you couldn't tune up with them. You never had enough slide to pull out. And you couldn't transpose enough to put him natural, or put you natural, and him transposed, or him natural, and you transposed. So we did without the piano. Like I tell you, they never even had any recording machines. Never had no, they never recorded no music at all. There was no records made in the city at that particular time. And that's why we didn't get down on plate. But I'm sorry I never had it at that time, because just to show a couple of the good brothers that thought they knew it all and composed pieces that played when they was running around in three corner pants. Go ahead, Crawford. Finish that. Okay. I wanted to ask you, after the war, you continued playing, but were you playing with brass bands or mostly just jazz bands? No, I had my own band. After the First World War. Yeah. I had my own band. What was it called? Mellow's Arrillo. Same as that chord that I showed you. I had Joe Castro on tuba. I had Joe Polizzi on clarinet. I had Bullshank on drums, Emil Bullshank on drums. I played cornet. Pete Dentron played cornet and I also played trombone. Who was going to? Joe Castro told me, and he told us the people over there, but we belonged to the, oh, can't think of the name of that president, club they had over there. But anyhow, he said that he made more money with me in one week than he made with Jacqueline in a month. We was going every night, every night in the week and in the day, Saturday and Sunday in the day. But then it tightened up on me in the tropics. So it was either case of wanting and I couldn't afford to turn $3,500 down for five months' work. So I left Pete Dentron under a band a while, but I don't know, they had a dissension and eventually disintegrated. Made money down there, made money here. Got a hell of a lot better then than I feel now. But they ain't got, I shouldn't feel that bad. If it wasn't for the sciatic and the other one, I'd be all right. But that horn that you've seen, that horn even touched his last, I don't know, I'm not playing. But that's a horn. That, did he play, he played pretty much until, you said a couple, three years before he died? Yeah, just about. And he was playing around here? Yeah, he was playing around here. Who did he play with? George Rispoy, and really I never, I never seen much allowance because I was out of town most. And I never seen much, I know he played with George Rispoy, I don't know. And, if ever I'd get up and play a piece of music in front of any gang, particularly that gang, at that famous jazz club, I'd like to dedicate the number I played to that the good brothers that played with me before I played with us and passed on. That goes for a whole lot of them. I think it's no more, that's a one-sided outfit. They used to send me cards and cards and cards and cards, but there ain't no use of me going up there. I'd only get myself in the jam. So I said, there's more big feeling musicians up there now. Jack Lane will tell you that. Lane told me, he told Benny Mars that one night, he says, you know, he said, as long as I got that thing in the band, he said, I'm a damn, but I'll never get another cornet. He said, one cornet's enough for ten, man. Now how you like that? But I had to look like that table. And I never did guitar, I couldn't guitar. And I love you. You got to love music to play music, and to play music, you got to love music.
